title: No sound of iron (1 Kings 6:7)
hookLine: the Temple is built without the sound of hammer or axe

cards: A building site is loud. Saws, drills, a radio, somebody shouting measurements across the lot. One verse in Kings describes a building site of a different kind: Solomon's house for God in Jerusalem.
Great stones going up, cedar beams, gold. And in the middle of the description, the text stops for what sounds like an aside. At the site itself, you couldn't hear the hammers.
Not because nobody cut stone. Because the cutting happened somewhere else.

teach.h: STONE MADE READY AT THE QUARRY.
teach.b: Here's the verse. The house was built of stone made ready before it was brought, and there was "neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house, while it was in building."
The Hebrew word for iron is barzel. The cutting happened at the quarry; at the holy place, the stones were only set. Why tell us?
The verse doesn't say. But some readers hear an echo from the Torah.

teach.h: NO TOOL LIFTED ON THE ALTAR.
teach.b: In Exodus, an altar of stone is built of stones no tool has been lifted against; lift your tool on it, the text says, and you have profaned it.

A later teaching in the Mishnah gives a reason: iron was made to shorten a person's life, and the altar was made to lengthen it, so the thing that shortens shouldn't be raised over the thing that lengthens.

teach.h: THE SHAMIR: A LEGEND OF SILENCE.
teach.b: And the Talmud tells a legend of the shamir, a tiny creature that could cut stone without any tool, so the work could go on in silence. That one is a story the rabbis tell, not a line in Kings.
Side by side, these readings point the same way: the metal that can shorten a life is kept away from the place built to lengthen it.

teach.h: NEITHER HAMMER NOR AXE NOR ANY TOOL OF IRON.
teach.b: The noise happened offstage, in the quarry. Here there was only placing, fitting, setting. Ordinary life has work like that too: the preparation done out of sight, the kind that's finished before anyone hears it.

how: Jews read of the Temple's building in the book of Kings, and the Mishnah's teaching about iron and the altar is studied in tractate Middot.

o: the cedar wood that lined the Temple's walls
iron, the metal no one heard at the Temple site
the gold that covered the Temple's inner room

games.q: no sound of iron — tap the pairs.
p: where the stones were made ready
stones no tool was lifted on
a legend: it cut stone in silence

s: Kings says the Temple was built with no tools at all
the stones were cut at the quarry. the text says no tool of iron was heard in the house.
the shamir legend comes from the Talmud, not from Kings
it's a story the rabbis tell; the verse in Kings only says no iron was heard.
the Mishnah links iron with shortening life
iron shortens life, it says, and the altar lengthens it.

games.q: you're building a house for God. the stones have to be cut somewhere. where do you shape them?
o: right at the site, so they fit perfectly.
at the quarry, so no iron is heard in the house.
nowhere: you use only uncut stone.
games.why: the text says the stone was made ready before it was brought, and no hammer, axe or tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built.

practice: Picture one task waiting for you, a sink of dishes, a report, a favor for someone, and see yourself doing it the Temple way: prepared beforehand, done without announcing it or telling anyone how hard it was.
Let this quiet minute be the quarry, where you get ready. If you pray, you can offer the work before you begin it.

wordCard.voice: Barzel. The Hebrew word for iron, the one tool and sound kept away from building the Temple. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: iron. no tool of barzel was heard in the house.

carryVoice: Your line: finished before anyone hears it. The noise belongs to the quarry. That's day seven hundred fifty-nine.
